attributes.title: Level 1

subgroups.name: build 1

steps.hints: ❓ Did you select the tan path tile in the Player sprite’s [place sprite on top of random tile] block?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:


Ask the ninja:

❓ What’s the difference between the [place sprite on top of] and the [place sprite on top of random tile] blocks?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Guide the ninja to notice that they can use the  [place sprite on top of] block to set a sprite’s specific location on the tilemap, whereas they can use the [place sprite on top of random tile] block if they want to set the sprite’s position randomly or on a particular kind of tile.

💡 Prompt the ninja to observe that the tilemap grid is larger than the controller’s screen and that sprites are able to move offscreen.
steps.instructions:
Begin the project by placing the Player sprite on the tilemap!


The starter code in this project provides you with the Player, Enemy, and Food sprites.


Open Scene and drag a [place sprite on top of random tile] block into the [on start] container under the Player sprite. Select the Player sprite and set the sprite’s starting position by clicking the gray box and selecting the tan path tile.


Click ▶ and move the Player sprite around the tilemap. Notice that the tilemap is larger than what the simulator shows.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you add a [camera follow sprite] code block and set the correct sprite name?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:


Ask the ninja:

❓ What do you notice about the size of the tilemap? 

❓ Why do you think the [camera follow sprite] block will be useful?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡Guide the ninja to see the connection to the [sprite stay in screen] block. Previously, if a sprite moved off screen, the ninja would not be able to see it. With the use of the [camera follow sprite] block, the ninja is able to follow the sprite, even when they move beyond the size of the screen.
steps.instructions:
Add a camera to follow the sprite!


Notice that the Player sprite is able to move off the viewable screen. Open Scene and drag a [camera follow sprite] block, then set it to the Player sprite.


Click ▶ and move the Player sprite around the tilemap. Notice that the camera follows the Player sprite to different parts of the tile map on the screen!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you select the correct sprite name and the tan path tile in both [place sprite on top of random tile] blocks in each [on game update every ms]?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:


Ask the ninja:

❓ Why would you want the two kinds of Food sprites to appear randomly on the tilemap?

❓ What happens when the Player sprite overlaps with the sprout Food sprite? What happens when the Player sprite overlaps with the carrot SpecialFood sprite?

❓How often should the two types of Food sprites appear on the screen?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Prompt the ninja to think about how they should adjust the interval of each [on game update every ms] loop if the sprout Food sprite should appear more often than the carrot SpecialFood sprite.
steps.instructions:
Randomize each Food sprite's starting positions!


Set the sprout Food sprite’s position by adding a [place sprite on top of random tile] block in the [on game update every ms] loop, selecting the Food sprite’s name, and selecting the tan path tile. Set the carrot SpecialFood sprite’s position by adding a [place sprite on top of random tile] block in the [on game update every ms] loop, selecting the SpecialFood sprite’s name, and selecting the tan path tile.


Adjust the parameter of the [on game update every ms] loop so that the two types of Food sprites appear at different intervals.


Click ▶ and move the Player sprite around the tilemap to “eat” the Food sprites!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you select the draw walls icon in the tilemap editor and click each section of green grass tiles until they are all highlighted in red?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:


Ask the ninja:

❓ Why might adding walls to your game make it more challenging?

❓Why do you think using the fill tool is sometimes more useful than individually clicking to fill tiles?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡If they wish, the ninja can also edit where the walls are located on the map. To do this, they can use the green grass tile to replace tan path tiles and then use the draw walls tool to turn them into walls.
steps.instructions:
Turn on the maze walls!


Click on the square in the [set tilemap to] block to edit. Notice the size of the tilemap in the bottom left of the tilemap editor: 16 by 16.


Notice that the green grass tiles are not marked as walls. Click the draw walls icon , then select the fill tool and click on the green grass tiles to turn them all into walls.


Click ▶ and notice that the game is more challenging now that the Player sprite needs to move around the walls to collect Food sprites.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you set the speed in the  [set sprite follow] block so that the Enemy sprite follows the Player sprite?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:


Ask the ninja:

❓ What speed should you set the Enemy sprite to so that the game is challenging, but not impossible?

❓ Why might it be helpful to place the Enemy sprite on a random tile, versus setting its position using tile coordinates?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡Remind the ninja to make sure that the correct sprites and tiles are selected in the [place sprite on top of random tile] and [set sprite follow] blocks.
steps.instructions:
Make the game a challenge by adding in a moving Enemy sprite! 


Set the Enemy sprite’s position by adding a [place sprite on top of random tile] block into the [on start] container, selecting the Enemy sprite’s name, and selecting the tan path tile.


Drag a [set sprite follow] block and set the Enemy sprite to follow the Player sprite. Set the speed to be challenging, but not impossible.


Click ▶ to see the Enemy sprite follow the Player sprite around the tilemap!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you add a [camera shake] block and [place sprite on random tile] block into the [on (Player) overlaps (Enemy)] container and adjust the parameters?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:



Ask the ninja:

❓What happens when you add the [camera shake] block into the [on (Player) overlaps (Enemy)] container?

❓How do different pixel and time parameters change the visual effect?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡Encourage the ninja to think of the camera shake of adding new effects to the game to make it more exciting. Prompt the ninja to think about what events might result in the screen being “shook.”
steps.instructions:
Make something happen when the Player sprite overlaps with the Enemy sprite!


The starter code already has an [on (Player) overlaps (Enemy)] container. 


Open Scene and drag out a [camera shake] block into the [on (Player) overlaps (Enemy)] container. Adjust the pixel and time parameters in the block and test out the code to see what effects make this project more fun!


Add a [place sprite on random tile] block and select the tan path tile to reset the Farmer sprite's position. Replace the sprite name with (otherSprite).


Click ▶ and notice what happens when the Player Sprite overlaps with the Enemy sprite!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you check that you placed each code block into the correct [on sprite overlaps sprite] container?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:


Ask the ninja:

❓ How many points should the Player sprite earn when they overlap the Food sprite? How many should they earn when they overlap the SpecialFood sprite?

❓ Did you select effect and time parameters that you like in the [destroy sprite] block?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Encourage the ninja to pay attention to the different [on sprite overlaps sprite] containers, as different things should happen when the Player sprite overlaps with sprites of different kinds.
steps.instructions:
Add score and life variables to make the project more exciting!


The starter code already has [set score to] and [set life to] blocks in the [on start] container. 


In both Food and SpecialFood [on sprite overlaps sprite] containers, add a [change score by] block. Change the parameter so that the SpecialFood sprite gives the Player sprite more points on overlap.


Then, add a [destroy sprite] block to both [on sprite overlaps sprite] containers, and replace (mySprite) by dragging (otherSprite) into the parameter. Click the + and select an effect and choose a time parameter of how long the effect lasts.


In the Player and Enemy [on (Player) overlaps (Enemy)] container, add a [change life by] block so that the life decreases on overlap. 


Click ▶ to see what happens to the Player’s score and life variables when they overlap with the Food, SpecialFood, and Enemy sprites.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you add fun customizations such as tilemap edits, splash or dialog text, animations, sounds, etc?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:


Ask the ninja:

❓How might you edit the tilemap to make the project more of your own? What tiles would you change? Where else can you add walls?

❓ What directions will help people understand how your project works?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Guide ninjas to note that while these customizing blocks are open ended and not required for the game to “work”, they really improve the Player’s experience playing a game, either by giving context to what the Player should do or not do, or to provide a more fun experience overall. They also allow the Ninja to add their personal touch and express themselves through small details present in the game.
steps.instructions:
Customize this game by adding directions at the beginning, animating different sprites, and adding music or screen effects. Be sure to edit the tiles and walls to make the game easier or more challenging!


Click ▶ to see the completed game project!

subgroups.introduction: Create a project that uses a tilemap, customizes walls, uses a camera view to “follow” a sprite around the tilemap, and resets sprite locations on the tilemap!

validationItems.text: Set the Player, Enemy, and Food sprites’ positions on random tan path tiles on the tilemap.
Use the camera to follow the Player sprite.
Set the Enemy to follow the Player sprite, at a challenging but not impossible speed.
Make the camera shake and the Enemy sprite reset to a random tan path tile when it overlaps a Player sprite.
Set score and life variables that change when the Player sprite overlaps other sprite kinds.

attributes.description: Welcome to Level 1 of Orange Belt! In this level, you’ll learn more about using tilemaps in your projects. You’ll also review sequence, which is the specific order of steps in code.
